To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have developed a web-based tool that predicts sites of ADAR-mediated editing in dsRNA.
the ADAR editing specificity depends on both the catalytic domain and the dsRNA binding domain, and that the editing specificity is determined by the local dsRNA context.

(i) ADARs prefer to edit adenosines with specific 5′ and adjacent 3′ bases; (ii) this specificity is mostly dictated by the enzymatic domain, but the dsRNA binding domain also influences 3′ neighbour choices for ADAR2; and (iii) the predictive power of our model on fully paired dsRNA is higher than on biological substrates containing bulges, mismatches and loops, suggesting structural contributions to editing site choice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
RNA editing and the development of algorithms for predicting RNA-editing sites.
the identification of RNA editing sites in double-stranded RNAs and the development of a predictive algorithm.
the identification of the factors that influence ADAR editing site choice and the development of a predictive tool that can be used in a variety of contexts.

ADARs are not very selective, but rather are able to edit a large number of sites in dsRNA.
ADARs are very specific and that the sequence context surrounding an editing site is the main determinant of editing efficiency.

ADAR editing site choice is dictated by the catalytically active site, with the 5′ neighbouring base having the strongest effect.

the 5′ and the 2nd nearest neighbours are the most important for predicting editing sites, and that mismatches, bulge and loop structures in the substrate can significantly affect the editing site preference.
